newsitem.title: USA: Jury sentences Oklahoma City bomber to death.
newsitem.headline: Jury sentences Oklahoma City bomber to death.

text.p: Embittered former soldier Timothy McVeigh was sentenced to death on Friday for blowing up a federal building in Oklahoma City, causing the deaths of 168 people in the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch solemnly read the jury's verdict, reached after 11 hours of deliberations over two days, to a packed courtroom.
The jury of seven men and five women convicted McVeigh on June 2 of 11 murder, conspiracy and explosives charges for bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995.
Prosecutors said McVeigh deserved to die for "the most bloody domestic terrorist act in the history of our country."

The defence pleaded for life imprisonment instead, saying McVeigh was a decent person who was deeply disturbed by the deaths of about 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a fiery confrontation with federal agents at Waco, Texas in 1993.
In a surprising twist, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones conceded McVeigh was guilty in his closing statement on Thursday. "He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic," Jones said.

He urged the jury to spare McVeigh, saying that if he was executed the full story of the bombing might never be known and other possible conspirators would never be brought to justice. "Dead men do not tell tales," Jones said.
The prosecution said the jury should have no mercy on McVeigh. "Tell him he is no patriot. He is a traitor and he deserves to die," prosecutor Beth Wilkinson said.

Law enforcement agents, office workers, visitors and 19 children were killed when a rented truck packed with a bomb made from ammonium nitrate fertiliser and fuel oil blew up outside the Murrah building, bringing down nine stories on the occupants.
The blast caused deep national shock and revulsion, smashing the myth that America's heartland was safe from indiscriminate attacks.
Prosecutors said McVeigh, a 29-year-old Gulf War veteran, was a right-wing fanatic who blew up the building to avenge the deaths at Waco two years earlier.
McVeigh did not testify at his trial and showed little emotion, sitting stiff and soldier-like at the defence table.

Prosecutors called emotional testimony from dozens of bombing survivors, victims' relatives and rescue workers during the penalty phase. They described the loss of their loved ones and the awful impact of the bombing on their lives.
A number of witnesses wept and several jurors wiped away tears during the testimony.
"I feel like my heart looks like that building and has a huge hole that never can be mended," said a weeping Diane Leonard, whose husband, Secret Service agent Donald Leonard, was killed.

Rescue workers told harrowing tales of pulling babies from the rubble. Police officer Alan Prokop said he carried out Brandon Denny, a young child who "appeared to have a brick stuck out of his forehead."

The defence called relatives, former Army colleagues, friends and neighbours to give a sympathetic picture of McVeigh's character and his youth in the small town of Pendleton, New York, where he displayed an early liking for guns.
They heaped praise on him, describing him as a cheerful child, an excellent student and outstanding soldier who tried to help others with their problems.
McVeigh's parents took the stand to plead for their son's life. "He is not the monster he has been portrayed as," said his tearful mother, Mildred Frazer.
